summary.countMeaning: 259 overlapping artifact review groups: 15 complete lesson bodies, 23 complete question items including every key/distractor, 21 formula cards and 200 complete glossary entries including aliases/examples. Errors corrected counts 47 finalized locations: 39 glossary fields in31 entries,5 lesson bodies and3 question fields. Reference refinements and contextual link corrections are included; this is not a fabricated count of individual atomic factual claims.

corrections.before: After free(s), the lifetime of *s has ended even though the pointer s still holds the old address.
corrections.after: After free(s), the lifetime of *s has ended. C makes pointers to that ended object indeterminate; do not inspect or dereference them as if they were valid addresses.

corrections.before: Calling greet() pushes a new stack frame holding buf[16]; returning pops it.
corrections.after: A conventional unoptimised greet call can use a frame holding buf[16]; optimisation and the ABI determine whether those objects and a separate frame remain.

corrections.before: The region where a program allocates memory at run time with malloc (or new in C++) and later frees it. Objects there live until explicitly freed, which is where use-after-free and double free bugs arise.
corrections.after: Dynamically allocated storage obtained through interfaces such as malloc in C or new in C++. It can occupy multiple mappings; allocated objects remain alive until released through the appropriate mechanism.

corrections.before: Overflowing name[16] into the neighbouring is_admin field grants access without touching any return address.
corrections.after: A possible threat scenario is an overflow from name[16] affecting a neighbouring is_admin decision without changing a return address; the invalid C copy has no guaranteed outcome.

corrections.before: A bug where a program writes past the end (or before the start) of a buffer, overwriting neighbouring memory. Depending on what lies next to the buffer, it can change data, crash the program or redirect execution.
corrections.after: A write outside a buffer's bounds, before its start or beyond its end. In C this is undefined behaviour: corrupting nearby data, crashing or redirecting execution are possible risks, not guaranteed traces.

corrections.before: Copying a 40-byte name into char buf[16] with strcpy writes 25 bytes past the end.
corrections.after: Copying a 40-byte name with strcpy needs 41 bytes including NUL, exceeding char buf[16] by 25; the invalid call has no promised overwrite trace.

corrections.before: An overflow that writes consecutive bytes onwards from the buffer, so it must pass through everything between the buffer and its target. A stack canary relies on this: the overflow has to cross the canary to reach the return address.
corrections.after: A write proceeding through consecutive locations beyond a buffer boundary. In a protected layout where a canary lies between that buffer and saved return information, reaching the latter crosses the guard; layouts and detection are not universal.

corrections.before: The C library function strcpy(dst, src) that copies a NUL-terminated string, including its NUL, into dst. It is never told dst's size, so too long a source overflows the destination.
corrections.after: The C library function strcpy(dst, src) copies a valid NUL-terminated source including its NUL into a sufficiently large, non-overlapping destination. It has no destination-capacity argument; violating those requirements gives undefined behaviour.

corrections.before: strcpy into char buf[8] from "ABCDEFGHIJ" needs 11 bytes and overflows by 3.
corrections.after: Copying "ABCDEFGHIJ" needs 11 bytes including NUL, exceeding char buf[8] by 3; no particular effect of that invalid call is promised.

corrections.before: A C library function that formats text into a buffer like printf but with no size limit, so long output overflows the buffer. snprintf is the bounded replacement.
corrections.after: A C library function formatting text into a destination without a capacity argument. The caller must provide enough valid storage for all output and its NUL; use snprintf with correct arguments and error/truncation handling to bound writes.

corrections.before: C types from <stdint.h> with an exact size: uint8_t is an unsigned 8-bit integer (1 byte), uint32_t 32 bits (4 bytes) and uint64_t 64 bits (8 bytes).
corrections.after: Optional exact-width unsigned C types from <stdint.h>: uint8_t has 8 value bits, uint32_t 32 and uint64_t 64. On an eight-bit-byte implementation their sizes are one, four and eight bytes; an implementation need not provide every exact-width type.

corrections.before: The natural integer and pointer size of a processor: 8 bytes (64 bits) on x86-64 and AArch64. The glibc stack canary is one machine word.
corrections.after: An architecture-dependent natural unit for registers and operations, whose meaning depends on context. x86-64 has 64-bit general-purpose registers; the illustrated glibc guard is a uintptr_t, eight bytes in the conventional 64-bit ABI. Other ABIs can use smaller pointers.

corrections.before: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word_(computer_architecture)
corrections.after: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bminor/glibc/master/sysdeps/generic/dl-osinfo.h

corrections.before: A freed session object's memory is reused for request bytes, and a stale check of s->is_admin reads the attacker's byte.
corrections.after: A possible threat scenario is a freed session's storage being reused for request bytes before a stale alias is accessed; C does not guarantee what the invalid access observes.

corrections.before: A C++ smart pointer that is the single owner of an object and frees it automatically when it goes out of scope. It cannot be copied, only moved, so ownership stays clear.
corrections.after: A move-only C++ smart pointer holding exclusive ownership through an associated deleter. Destruction or reset invokes that deleter for its managed object; release instead transfers the stored pointer without destroying the object. Borrowed aliases still need lifetime discipline.

corrections.before: A %-sequence in a printf format string that tells printf to consume an argument, such as %s (a string), %d (an integer), %x (hexadecimal) or %n (store the number of characters printed so far through a pointer).
corrections.after: A %-sequence in a printf format string. Conversions such as %s, %d and %x consume arguments of specified types, and %n stores the emitted character count through a pointer; %% instead emits a literal percent sign without consuming an argument.

corrections.before: Unused bytes the compiler inserts between or after a struct's fields so each field is aligned. Their contents are not set by assigning the fields, so copying the raw struct out can leak old memory.
corrections.after: Bytes between or after structure members that are not part of those members, commonly needed for alignment. C gives padding unspecified values when structure or member values are stored, so member assignments do not establish safe contents for a raw copy across a trust boundary.

corrections.before: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public catalogue that gives each known security vulnerability a unique identifier such as CVE-2014-0160 (Heartbleed).
corrections.after: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a programme assigning identifiers and publishing records for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. A CVE ID such as CVE-2014-0160 identifies one record; not every known vulnerability necessarily has an ID or a published record.

corrections.before: The GNU Compiler Collection, a widely used open-source compiler for C, C++ and other languages; the default compiler on most Linux distributions.
corrections.after: The GNU Compiler Collection, an open-source compiler collection supporting C, C++ and other languages. Its flags and enabled protections depend on the compiler version, target and build configuration.

corrections.before: The GNU C Library, the standard C library on most Linux systems. It provides malloc, strcpy, printf and also stack-canary set-up and source fortification.
corrections.after: The GNU C Library, a C library implementation used by GNU/Linux systems. It provides interfaces such as malloc, strcpy and printf, and implementation support for stack guards and source fortification. Other Linux systems can use another C library.

corrections.before: The C standard library a program links against, providing functions such as malloc, printf and memcpy; on most Linux systems it is glibc. It is mapped into almost every process, which makes it a favourite target for code reuse.
corrections.after: A C library implementation providing interfaces such as malloc, printf and memcpy. It can be linked dynamically or statically; glibc is one GNU/Linux implementation. Known code in a loaded library may be used by code-reuse attacks.

corrections.before: A short instruction sequence already in executable memory that ends in a return instruction. Chained together, gadgets let an attacker perform arbitrary operations without injecting code.
corrections.after: An existing instruction sequence ending in a return, used as a building block in a return-oriented program. Which operations an attacker can compose depends on the available sequences, controllable state and effective protections.

corrections.before: The machine instruction that returns from a function by taking the return address from the stack and jumping to it.
corrections.after: In x86, an instruction returning from a function by taking the return address from the ordinary stack, with additional checks when features such as CET shadow stacks are enabled. Other architectures can use a return instruction that takes its target from a register instead.

corrections.before: The distance in bytes from the start of something, such as a struct or a library, to an item inside it. Library offsets are fixed for a given build, so base + offset gives an item's address.
corrections.after: A distance from a specified origin, usually measured in bytes for a structure field or mapped image. Adding a known target's relative offset to the matching fixed-layout image base locates it; separately allocated or specially resolved objects need different reasoning.

corrections.before: Patching addresses in a program or library when it is loaded, because the final location of code and data, especially with ASLR, is only known then.
corrections.after: Adjusting address-dependent values when code or data is placed at its final location. Linkers can apply relocations while producing an executable, and dynamic loaders apply the relevant remaining relocations when objects are loaded.

corrections.before: The 64-bit version of Intel and AMD's x86 processor architecture, used in most PCs and servers. It is little-endian.
corrections.after: The 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction-set architecture, implemented by Intel and AMD processors among others. It uses little-endian byte order; a chosen ABI determines the sizes of C types and pointers.

corrections.before: A C++ method call dispatched at run time through a table of function pointers (the vtable), so it is an indirect call that CFI can protect.
corrections.after: A C++ call selecting the appropriate virtual-function overrider from an object's dynamic type unless dispatch is suppressed or optimised away. Common ABIs implement dynamic dispatch with a virtual table; the C++ language does not require that representation.

corrections.before: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtual_function
corrections.after: https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2023/n4950.pdf

corrections.before: Branch Target Identification, an Armv8.5-A feature: on protected pages, indirect branches must land on a BTI landing-pad instruction, otherwise the CPU faults.
corrections.after: Branch Target Identification, introduced in Armv8.5-A: covered indirect branches into guarded pages must reach a compatible landing pad when checking is enabled. Accepted instructions and branch classes matter; some pointer-authentication instructions also serve as landing pads.

corrections.before: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/AArch64-Options.html
corrections.after: https://llvm.org/doxygen/AArch64BranchTargets_8cpp_source.html

corrections.before: The x86 instruction that marks a valid target for indirect branches under Intel IBT. On processors without IBT it does nothing.
corrections.after: The x86-64 ENDBR instruction marking a valid indirect-branch target when Intel IBT checking applies. With IBT disabled it has no such checking effect; ENDBR32 is the distinct form for 32-bit code.

corrections.before: https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/endbr64
corrections.after: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/llvm/llvm-project/main/llvm/lib/Target/X86/X86IndirectBranchTracking.cpp

corrections.before: A marked location accepted by a relevant indirect-branch protection, such as an ENDBR instruction for Intel IBT or a compatible Arm BTI instruction. Acceptance depends on the architecture's branch class, enforcement and configuration; it does not generally prove the intended function type.
corrections.after: A marked location accepted by an enabled indirect-branch protection. Intel IBT uses ENDBR instructions; Arm BTI accepts compatible BTI instructions and some pointer-authentication instructions. Acceptance depends on branch class and configuration and does not establish an intended function type.

corrections.before: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/AArch64-Options.html
corrections.after: https://llvm.org/doxygen/AArch64BranchTargets_8cpp_source.html

corrections.before: With 16 possible tags, a stale pointer matches a randomly retagged granule 1 time in 16.
corrections.after: Only under an independent uniform choice among all sixteen tags does one stale tag match with probability one in sixteen; allocator policies can differ.

corrections.before: The compiler stage that produces machine instructions from a program; its output is the generated code. Protections such as stack canaries and pointer authentication are added here, so they cover only the code the compiler built with them.
corrections.after: The compiler stage producing machine instructions from a program. Compiler-generated checks protect the covered generated operations; hand-written assembly, separately compiled code and runtime enablement can require separate arrangements.

changes.before: floor: round down to a whole number, which is what C's integer division does for non-negative values
changes.after: floor: round down to a whole number; C discards the fractional remainder for the non-negative values used here

changes.before: Apply input limits and handle allocation failure
changes.after: Apply application-specific count limits and handle allocation failure

changes.before: A linear overflow from `buf` must pass through the canary to reach the return address.
changes.after: In the illustrated layout, a linear overflow from `buf` must pass through the canary to reach the return address.

changes.before: overflows within a struct (field order is fixed by the language)
changes.after: overwrites confined to fields within a struct (field order is fixed by the language)

corrections.before: What is ASLR's main contribution to stopping exploitation?
corrections.after: What is ASLR's main contribution against a memory-corruption attack?

changes.before: An indirect call (`fp()`, a C++ virtual call) should only reach functions that could validly be called there.
changes.after: An indirect call such as `fp()` obtains its target at run time. C++ virtual dispatch commonly also uses indirect calls, though the compiler can devirtualise a call when it knows the target. A forward-edge check restricts the covered transfer to its permitted target set.

changes.before: though the compiler can devirtualise a call when it knows the target
changes.after: though a compiler knowing the target can replace dynamic dispatch with a direct call

corrections.before: An attacker has bypassed ASLR with a leak and uses a stack buffer overflow (with the canary also leaked) to chain together snippets of existing libc code, each ending in `ret`. Assuming it is supported and enabled for the relevant code, which mitigation checks these forged returns?
corrections.after: An attacker has bypassed ASLR with a leak and uses a stack buffer overflow (with the canary also leaked) to chain together snippets of existing libc code, each ending in `ret`. Assuming it is supported and enabled for the relevant code, which mitigation checks these modified returns?

corrections.before: Correct. CFG checks indirect call targets against a bitmap of valid function starts.
corrections.after: CFG validates covered indirect-call targets against a table of permitted target addresses. It is a forward-edge policy; an allowed address is not a proof of the intended function type.

changes.before: Extra vulnerabilities are sometimes needed for exploitation
changes.after: Extra vulnerabilities are sometimes needed to turn a bug into an attack

corrections: sys-elf-hardening: 'at -O0 the tested glibc 2.39 and 2.41 headers silently leave fortification off' (implied glibc is silent) -> upstream glibc headers warn that _FORTIFY_SOURCE requires optimisation (since 2.16, still in 2.42/master); Debian and Ubuntu packages remove that warning, so there the checks are silently absent.

sys-mitigations-q7 workedExample: same claim (silent with glibc 2.39/2.41 headers) -> upstream warns, Debian/Ubuntu remove the warning; the -O0 binary calls plain strcpy either way. The author had removed '(and recent versions warn)', which was in fact correct for upstream glibc.

sys-elf-hardening: 'In a GCC 14 test on Linux, the fragment's flags produced both' -> GCC 13 on x86-64 produced both with the full fragment; GCC on 64-bit Arm rejects -fcf-protection=full, and a GCC 14 Arm build without it also produced both.

sys-object-ownership: 'Java's garbage collector reclaims objects automatically and never explicitly frees them' (self-contradictory) -> Java programs never free objects explicitly; a garbage collector reclaims only objects nothing can still reach. Borrow-checker sentence widened to include references that outlive their value (E0597).

sys-stack-canaries: unqualified 'With glibc the process prints *** stack smashing detected ***: terminated' -> 'With glibc 2.31 or later ... (older versions also printed the program name)'; tests named as GCC 13 and GCC 14.
glossary sys-sigabrt example hedged to glibc 2.31 or later.
sys-buffer-bounds analogy: '16-letter box' could suggest 16 characters fit -> box of 16 squares, and the limit now says the NUL needs one square so 16 bytes hold only 15 letters.

sys-elf-hardening.rationale: No maths. FORTIFY facts checked against glibc sources: SIGABRT on failure (glibc manual D.2); level 3 only for GCC >= 12 or Clang >= 9, otherwise treated as 2 with a warning (features.h, commits c43c579 and 86bf0fe). Verifier CORRECTED the -O0 claim: upstream glibc headers have warned '_FORTIFY_SOURCE requires compiling with optimization (-O)' since 2.16 (commit 05c2c96, BZ 13979) and still do in 2.39, 2.41, 2.42 and master; Debian/Ubuntu's patch any/local-revert-bz13979.diff removes the warning, which is why the author's Debian 2.41 and Ubuntu 2.39 tests were silent. Reproduced: no warning with the distro headers, and the upstream form of features.h makes GCC 14 ('#warning ... [-Wcpp]') and Clang 19 ('[-W#warnings]') warn; nm shows plain strcpy at -O0. Verifier also corrected the build-fragment test claim: GCC 14 on arm64 rejects -fcf-protection=full; the full fragment on x86-64 GCC 13.3 gives FLAGS BIND_NOW, FLAGS_1 NOW PIE, GNU_RELRO and IBT/SHSTK properties; arm64 GCC 14 without that flag gives BIND_NOW and GNU_RELRO; -no-pie -z lazy -z norelro gives neither.

Prompt, options and answer (1) unchanged; option 1 confirmed by features.h (__OPTIMIZE__ > 0 required).

Visible paragraph that mitigations restrict/detect while fixing bugs or memory-safe languages remove the corruption is consistent with the CISA roadmap.

analogyReview.scope: All 15 active lessons: 12 added analogies (mapping and limit checked against the primary sources listed) and 3 not-needed decisions; no question prompt or option contains an analogy, and no question-critical fact is only inside a callout.

sys-buffer-bounds.rationale: Paper form with fixed boxes: name box next to a 'Staff use: approved' box; strcpy as a pen not told where the box ends. Verifier changed '16-letter box' to 16 squares and added the NUL limit so the analogy cannot teach the off-by-one; limits (adjacency chosen by compiler/ABI/allocator, undefined behaviour) are accurate.

sys-bounded-strings.rationale: Short API-contract lesson (snprintf return, strncpy no NUL); the previous lesson's form analogy already covers bounded writes and the strncpy warning is clearer stated directly.

sys-heartbeat-lengths.rationale: Receptionist reading back a message by its claimed length: maps claimed length vs arrived payload and neighbouring heap; limits (heap not a tidy pile, read may fault, ~64 KB per reply) match RFC 6520, the OpenSSL advisory and heartbleed.com.

sys-allocation-arithmetic.rationale: Odometer rollover (99,990 + 16 -> 00,006) maps to the dropped carry bit of a 32-bit size_t product; limit (binary, nothing notices unless the code checks) accurate.

sys-object-ownership.rationale: Hotel key card not re-coded maps to a dangling pointer to reused storage; limit (free does nothing to held pointers, reuse is allocator-dependent, UB) accurate. Memory-safe-language facts are all outside the callout.

sys-format-input.rationale: Mail-merge template filled from user text maps to the format string as template; limit (printf has no list of supplied arguments; missing argument is UB; %n write) accurate.

sys-padding-disclosure.rationale: The visible byte-layout table is the concrete model; an everyday comparison would add nothing beyond it.

sys-finding-memory-bugs.rationale: Tool-selection lesson; its key limit (evidence only for executed paths/checked properties) is stated directly and needs no analogy.

sys-stack-canaries.rationale: Numbered seal across a storeroom door checked on rounds maps to a canary before the return address checked at protected exits; limits (leaked number, window = non-linear write, theft before the round, checks only at exits) match the lesson and GCC docs.

sys-nx-code-reuse.rationale: Ransom note cut from magazines maps to ROP gadgets in existing executable code chained by stack addresses; limits (attacker must learn addresses: ASLR; CPU can check returns: shadow stacks) accurate.

sys-aslr-guess-models.rationale: Fixed-code bike lock vs an imaginary self-resetting lock maps to fixed vs re-randomised bases; note nearby = information leak; limits (wrong ASLR guesses crash and are noticeable; no time model) accurate. q5's needed facts are in the visible bullets.

sys-aslr-pointer-leaks.rationale: Terrace of houses placed as one block maps to a mapping base plus fixed offsets; limits (other mappings, other builds) match the lesson's visible list.

sys-elf-hardening.rationale: Pencilled phone list laminated after a morning lookup maps to lazy vs eager binding plus RELRO; limits (other function pointers, dlopen'd libraries, start-up cost) match ld docs and q8.

sys-control-transfer-checks.rationale: Taxi with a sealed pickup logbook and approved destination list maps to shadow stack (backward edge) and forward-edge CFI, with landing-pad vs type-based policies; limits (allowed-but-wrong target, unprotected code or disabled enforcement) accurate.

sys-tagging-layers.rationale: Festival wristband colours recoloured when an area reopens maps to allocation/pointer tags and retagging on reuse; limits (16 colours collide, unchecked accesses, same-granule overflow, async reporting) match Android and kernel MTE docs.
